scenes.title: Ask BC — inside the BigCommerce control panel
scenes.caption: This is Ask BC — and the important thing is where it lives. It's right here inside the BigCommerce admin. Not a separate app, not a new tab. <break time="0.5s" /> That green dot means we have a live WebSocket connection to a Cloudflare Worker — a persistent connection to a Durable Object that holds this merchant's session. <break time="0.3s" /> Let me show you what it can do.

scenes.title: One question, six metrics
scenes.caption: I asked for a store summary. What came back isn't a wall of text — those are real React components, rendering inline. <break time="0.4s" /> Functionally, the merchant got their answer in about six seconds — instead of clicking through four different admin pages. Technically, the agent wrote one TypeScript script that called four APIs in parallel and computed the totals in memory. That's the Codemode advantage — one execution replaces what would have been ten serial tool calls.

scenes.title: Structured tables with follow-up suggestions
scenes.caption: Now a products table with real SKUs, right-aligned prices. But look below it — follow-up suggestions, generated from the response content. <break time="0.3s" /> The merchant doesn't have to think about what to ask next. That's the difference between a chatbot and an assistant — an assistant anticipates the next question. And there's copy and feedback buttons on every response, because the merchant owns this data.

scenes.title: Three-way join
scenes.caption: This is the query that breaks traditional agent architectures. <break time="0.4s" /> Five completed orders — each with per-line-item detail — from three different API surfaces, joined in memory, with computed totals. On a tool-calling agent, this would chain seven or eight serial round-trips and probably hit a step limit before finishing. <break time="0.3s" /> With Codemode, the model writes one script that fetches everything in parallel and returns structured tables. The model plans the entire query graph upfront — instead of discovering it one call at a time.

scenes.title: Transparent tool usage
scenes.caption: Every response shows which tools the agent called. This matters for trust — when an AI tells a merchant their revenue number, the merchant needs to know where that came from. Expand the indicator, see the exact APIs. <break time="0.3s" /> It's also a debugging surface for us. If the agent gives a wrong answer, we can trace which tools it used and what data it saw.

scenes.title: Write operations — preview before execution
scenes.caption: Now the agent isn't just reading — it's about to change the store. I said create a coupon. <break time="0.4s" /> And it did something important — it previewed the operation first. Showed me the exact arguments. Code, discount type, amount. And asked to confirm. <break time="0.3s" /> Functionally, the merchant stays in control. Technically, write tools use a two-turn pattern — the first call returns a preview, the second call actually executes. The store doesn't change until the merchant says yes.

scenes.title: Confirmed and created
scenes.caption: I confirmed, and the coupon is now live in BigCommerce. <break time="0.3s" /> That's a real coupon — I can verify it in the marketing section right now. Architecturally — write tools live outside the Codemode sandbox. The model can't accidentally trigger a write from inside generated code. Every mutation flows through an explicit tool call with typed arguments and an audit log.

scenes.title: How-to questions
scenes.caption: And it's not just data. I asked how to set up free shipping — and instead of a generic answer, it gave three concrete options with specific navigation paths in the admin. <break time="0.3s" /> Then offered to create the coupon right there in the chat. One surface for what is my store doing — and how do I make my store do something different.

scenes.title: Why Codemode
scenes.caption: Here's the architectural core. <break time="0.4s" /> The model writes TypeScript — not tool calls. That code runs in a sandboxed Dynamic Worker with zero network access. The only way out is typed RPC functions that resolve back to the host worker, which holds the merchant's access token. <break time="0.3s" /> The token never appears in generated code. This is the same credential isolation architecture Cloudflare uses in Agent Lee.

scenes.title: The architecture
scenes.caption: Two services, clear responsibilities. <break time="0.3s" /> Vercel handles what it's good at — OAuth, server-rendered pages, the iframe, React components. Cloudflare handles what it's good at — long-lived WebSocket connections, per-tenant Durable Objects, sub-ten-millisecond sandbox execution. <break time="0.3s" /> Credentials are encrypted at rest and resolved per merchant at runtime. Every piece of this scales to a thousand stores without code changes.

scenes.title: Twenty-nine curated tools
scenes.caption: Twenty-nine tools, all generated from BigCommerce's own OpenAPI specs. <break time="0.3s" /> Twenty-two read tools inside the Codemode sandbox. Seven write tools outside it with two-turn confirmation. <break time="0.4s" /> The curation matters — we taught the model that version two orders return bare arrays with string-typed numbers, that status ID ten means completed, that the coupons endpoint requires an applies-to field. That domain knowledge is what makes the agent work on the first try.

scenes.title: Your store, operating itself
scenes.caption: That's Ask BC. <break time="0.5s" /> The merchant doesn't learn a new tool — they just talk to the one they already have. Every BigCommerce store gets an AI operator that reads, writes, and explains — from a single marketplace install. <break time="0.4s" /> Codemode plus curated tools plus generative UI. That's the pattern. It works.
